There were 344 crypto security incidents in the first half of 2026 alone, that's almost two a day.

Here's why this keeps happening in crypto ↓

1️⃣ One bug = millions at risk

Protocols move money automatically, and a loophole in the code can let attackers drain funds before anyone notices.

2️⃣ Oracle manipulation

Manipulated price feeds can make a lending protocol value a token at 10x its actual price, letting attackers borrow way more than their collateral should allow.

3️⃣ Admin keys still exist

Even decentralized projects often have a few people with privileged access. Stolen keys or malicious approvals can give attackers control without exploiting a bug in the code.

4️⃣ Dependencies create new attack surfaces

Bridges, oracles, external contracts. Each adds another layer of risk, exposing even well-built protocols to failures elsewhere.

5️⃣ Audits are a snapshot, not a guarantee

An audit checks code at one point in time. It can miss edge cases, and later updates or integrations can introduce new vulnerabilities.

6️⃣ Asymmetric incentives

Security practices vary, and some teams run bug bounties and formal verification while others ship fast and hope for the best.

Meanwhile, attackers (including state-backed groups) have millions in upside and keep probing for weak points.

My take: defenders have to get a lot of things right. Attackers only need to find one weakness.

That’s why security can’t end with an audit. It has to keep up with every upgrade, integration, and person who has access to the funds.

I've been seeing comparisons between @worldnetwork and @Concordium on my TL for the past few days.

Most people get the idea wrong.

Both are building trust infrastructure for AI agents, but in very different ways.

World uses iris biometrics to prove someone is a unique human. Its AgentKit extends that human proof to agents.

Concordium is an AI project where identity sits in the protocol itself, so you can prove who's behind a wallet or an AI agent.

Its Agent Registry links agents to verified people or businesses, while ZK proofs let users prove attributes without exposing the underlying identity, and $CCD pays network fees.

Proving you’re over 18 without revealing your birth date is a good example.

As AI agents start holding wallets and moving money, proving who stands behind them becomes critical.
